notes: Same evening as the fish lesson (9–10): Myrddin went to the river without his hat (Pennod 9) and left it by the kitchen fire; Dafi ran home ahead of them (he cannot really fly: Pennod 9, 16; s015 'Mae e wedi rhedeg i'r llys'); Cai had ridden home early and was in the hall. The children address Myrddin as chi (eich het chi).

Target: wedi with every person (Dw i wedi, Rwyt ti wedi, Mae … wedi, Dyn ni wedi, Maen nhw wedi; Wyt ti wedi …?; Dw i ddim wedi; Dyw … ddim wedi). Contrasts with yn: Dafi's deliberate error ('Dafi'n bwyta pasteiod' → Mali: 'rwyt ti wedi bwyta'r pasteiod') and Cai's 'Wyt ti wedi bwyta, Cai? — Nac ydw! Dw i'n bwyta nawr!'. The only sy-clauses are the whitelisted Beth sy wedi digwydd? / Pwy sy wedi …?.

Myrddin's bargain is a present assignment and a command, as the plan asks ('Nawr mae gwaith gyda Dafi: cynnau'r ffwrn. Cynna'r tân, Dafi!'); there is no future or habitual time (bob bore waits for 18). Dafi only manages the flame when Modlen raises her spoon (fire when frightened). Modlen keeps the secret from Cynyr ('Dim byd, Cynyr!'). Callbacks to Pennod 7: 'ffwrn fach yw Dafi', Modlen's 'Cer mas!', Arth's 'Cath yw e'.
Running words 1102 (target 1000, window 900–1100): two words over after the Pennod 9 recall additions (o lan yr afon); not trimmed further.
New form licensed in the delta: cynna (imperative of cynnau).

Deliberate error (§6.4, s076): Dafi uses the progressive 'Dafi'n bwyta pasteiod' where the perfect is meant; Mali corrects it in the next line (s078 'rwyt ti wedi bwyta'r pasteiod'). Codex review 2026-10-12 accepts the contrast and the corrective Nage.

Codex review 2026-10-12, verdicts on the [?] questions (all accepted, no text change): s001 'Mae'r haul wedi mynd' (understandable in the nightfall context; machlud not available); s013 het f. → hi; s052 'Nage, Cai' (Na also possible); s060 'Oes, ond …' after 'Mae cynffon gyda Pero'; s079 'trwyn wrth drwyn' (established usage); s098 informal imperative 'Cynna'r tân!' (attested); s104 yn barod 'already' beside 'ready' elsewhere; s016 rhetorical fragment; s024 jwg masculine, pl. jygiau (sources differ; keep the course's masculine).

Applied from the Codex review (2026-10-12): s118 eto = 'yet' recorded as a second sense in the delta (cy-eto-s2, card stage 'yet'); Gramadeg rule and yn ↔ wedi table no longer define wedi as 'does dim … nawr', third row now Mae'r ffwrn wedi cynnau, 'chi' row added; A.a8 now cued by 'Nac ydw!' so only yn fits; B.b8 cued by 'Ha! Ha!'; B.b10 accepts golchi; C.c1, C.c5, C.c6 accept full-sentence answers.

Audit-fix pass 2026-10-19 (docs/reviews/welsh-russian-lessons-2026-10-19.md): s131 no longer repeats Pennod 6's closing gag (Pero sad / Dafi full and warm in the hat); Pero now glares at Myrddin's hat. s092 cynnau gloss no longer uses poeth before its first use (s104). Redundant Atishŵ gloss removed (s083 already says tisian). Pensa C.c1, C.c5, C.c6 accept further full answers (gyda Pero; Dafi sy wedi …; Mae Dafi'n cynnau'r ffwrn).

Owner fix 2026-11-04: Pensum C converted to open self_check questions in story order (c1, c2, c4, c5, c6, c8, c7; all self_check with rubric, key_terms and sources; c1, c5 and c6 converted from exact, accepted_answers removed). c3 ('Ydy Pero wedi bwyta'r pasteiod? Pam?') dropped so that only one Pam? item remains; c4 turned from a Pam? item into 'Ble mae'r olion yn mynd?'; new c8 'Pam mae Dafi'n cynnau'r ffwrn?' is the single late Pam?; c7 'A ti?' changed from 'Wyt ti wedi bwyta heddiw? Beth?' (a bare yes/no with a follow-up that fails after Nac ydw; 'Beth wyt ti wedi bwyta?' would need an object question not yet in the prose) to the open 'Ble wyt ti wedi bod heddiw?'. Rubrics now check one feature each. No exact key in A or B contains A ti?, so no A thi? variants were needed. nodyn_en expanded to a full English explanation (704 words). The checker's 60-word nodyn_en cap is advisory (RULES §6: length follows content). Codex review fixes (2026-11-04): perfect and yn ↔ wedi wording made less categorical (the perfect looks back from the present; the yn pattern also covers states and habits); eto 'yet' tied to its example, not to ddim; constructed table rows removed (chi row, Mae'r ffwrn wedi cynnau, Ydy Pero wedi …?) and the note now cites only attested sentences; sy wording revised; c7 sources s053 as the wedi bod model. The story's 1101 running words (one over the 900–1100 window) are left as they are: released prose is not cut or padded for one word.

Quality continuation audit, review 1104-202415-8377: first-use tired/flour/soup meaning aids and corrected introduction pointers; unique B3/B10 cues; explicit completed-action A7 cue and accurate hint; copied A8 recombined; linking-versus-locative yn claim narrowed; misleading negative table heading made neutral; Cynyr speaker added. English cues and long-note warnings intentional. Missing chi scope, Cynyr secrecy staging and legacy A contrast/format remain owner decisions; no scene reordered.

cover.alt: The llys kitchen in chaos at night: flour everywhere, a broken milk jug, a cauldron of burnt cawl with a knife in it, an empty pie board, and Modlen shouting with her wooden spoon raised as Myrddin and two dripping children appear in the doorway.
cover.art_brief: Llys kitchen at night (match place-cegin.png): timber posts, limewash, thatch, firelight from the hearth, the clay bread oven in the wall dark and cold. Total chaos: white flour over the long table, the bench, the chairs and the floor rushes; an overturned earthenware milk jug broken in a white puddle; a big iron cauldron of blackened, smoking cawl hanging on the hearth chain with the handle of a large kitchen knife sticking out of it; an empty wooden pie board with crumbs; a bare meat hook. Modlen (short, round, rosy, white headscarf, floury apron, brown dress with rolled sleeves) stands in the middle, wooden spoon raised like a sceptre, mouth open in a shout. In the yard doorway, against the dark blue night: Myrddin (very old, thin, long white beard, round wire spectacles, patched deep-blue robe, bareheaded), Arth (11, untidy brown hair with cowlick, oversized moss-green tunic) and Mali (12, long dark braid, dark-blue dress), the two children dripping wet, and Pero (big shaggy black-and-white hound, wet). Myrddin's tall black brimmed hat sits on a stool by the hearth; the very tip of a small red tail hangs over its brim. Llys palette. No text.

grammar.nodyn_en:
This chapter's new pattern is the perfect: the verb form that looks back from the present at something that has happened. In this chapter it usually presents a completed event whose result is still in view. Welsh builds it by putting wedi in the place of yn. Mae Dafi'n bwyta'r pasteiod means 'Dafi is eating the pies'; Mae Dafi wedi bwyta'r pasteiod! means 'Dafi has eaten the pies!'. So Mae'r jwg wedi torri ('The jug has broken'; English often says 'is broken').

A verb-noun is the dictionary form of a verb, such as bwyta ('to eat'): the form that follows yn in Mae Dafi'n bwyta. The same verb-noun follows wedi, and it never mutates (never changes its first sound): wedi bwyta, wedi torri ('has eaten, has broken'). The linking yn before a verb-noun commonly contracts to 'n after a vowel (locative yn remains distinct, as in Dyn ni yn yr afon, ‘We are in the river’), but wedi simply replaces the linking yn, with no 'n left over: Mae Dafi wedi bwyta ('Dafi has eaten'), never Mae Dafi'n wedi.

Everything before wedi stays as in the yn sentences of Penodau 3, 5 and 9; only yn changes. Dw i wedi bod yn bysgodyn! ('I've been a fish!'), Rwyt ti wedi blino ('You're tired'), Dyn ni wedi bod yn yr afon gyda Pero! ('We've been in the river with Pero!'), Maen nhw wedi mynd, Cai! ('They've gone, Cai!'). Bod is the verb-noun 'to be', so wedi bod means 'has been, have been'. The story has no chi form with wedi yet. The first table sets the two patterns side by side: Dyn ni'n glanhau'r gegin nawr ('We're cleaning the kitchen now'), and when the work is done, Mae'r plant wedi glanhau'r gegin ('The children have cleaned the kitchen').

Questions and negatives also work as before, because the verb at the front is still a form of bod. Myrddin asks Wyt ti wedi dysgu rhywbeth, Arth? ('Have you learnt something?'), and Arth answers Ydw ('Yes'). Modlen asks Wyt ti wedi bwyta'r pasteiod? ('Have you eaten the pies?') and Cai answers Nac ydw! ('No!'). In the negative, ddim comes before wedi: Dw i ddim wedi bwyta'r pasteiod ('I haven't eaten the pies').

Two questions are learnt whole for now: Beth sy wedi digwydd? ('What has happened?') and Pwy sy wedi bwyta'r pasteiod? ('Who has eaten the pies?'). In these questions, beth or pwy asks which thing or person did it, and sy is the form of bod used in that pattern; treat them as fixed phrases. The answers use the ordinary pattern: Mae rhywbeth wedi digwydd ('Something has happened').

Choosing between yn and wedi is a matter of meaning, not of a time word. In this chapter yn shows an action in progress, and wedi looks back at one that has been completed (elsewhere the yn pattern can also describe states and habits). Nawr ('now') appears with both: Dw i'n bwyta nawr! ('I'm eating now!') and nawr mae'r pasteiod wedi mynd ('now the pies have gone'). When Dafi says Dafi'n bwyta pasteiod ('Dafi eating pies'), the pies are already gone, so Mali corrects him: rwyt ti wedi bwyta'r pasteiod ('you have eaten the pies').

Wedi blino means 'tired' (literally 'having tired'), and wedi takes the place of yn here too: mae'r plant yn wlyb ac wedi blino ('the children are wet and tired'). Yn barod is a fixed phrase meaning 'ready' (Ydy'r cawl yn barod? 'Is the cawl ready?') or 'already' (Mae'r ffwrn yn boeth yn barod! 'The oven is hot already!'). In Dw i ddim wedi gwneud y cawl eto ('I haven't made the cawl yet'), eto means 'yet'; its other uses in this chapter, such as mae hi'n codi'r llwy eto ('she raises the spoon again'), mean 'again'.

The last table gathers mutations met in earlier chapters. After fy ('my') comes the nasal mutation (c becomes ngh, p becomes mh): fy nghegin i ('my kitchen'), fy mhasteiod i ('my pies'). After dy ('your') and ei ('his') comes the soft mutation, a softening of the first sound (t becomes d, p becomes b, c becomes g): dy drwyn di ('your nose', from trwyn), ei ben e ('his head', from pen), ei gynffon e ('his tail', from cynffon). After yn, an adjective softens too, except one beginning with ll or rh: yn ddig ('angry', from dig), yn boeth ('hot', from poeth).

Reference translations: Wyt ti wedi bwyta, Cai? — “Have you eaten, Cai?”; Mae’r cawl wedi llosgi — “The soup has burnt”; wedi llosgi — “has/have burnt”.
